Yet, standard weighted arithmetic mean aggregation in current DML systems may lead to considerable model inaccuracies and slow convergence speeds over fluctuating networks. In this paper, we introduce a new family of nonlinear aggregation functions to improve DML efficiency in networks subject to change. Our model utilizes a nonlinear weighted power mean aggregation approach instead of the linear aggregation typically employed by previous studies. By using mirror descent based on Bregman divergence for optimization and non-linear aggregation, we maintain the ability to reach an optimal solution. Our experiments further demonstrate that the new aggregation method has numerous advantages over existing linear aggregation methods.

This study aims to develop a maintenance model that takes into account the different levels of code sharing among software projects. These levels are determined by analyzing commit histories and repository connections, providing insights into the extent of code sharing within a community. By employing a random sampling approach, we selected 50 software projects from GitHub and calculated their respective code sharing indices. These projects were then grouped into different levels of code sharing, with a maintenance model developed for each category. Our results indicate that, in general, it is challenging for software developers to locate and update the original source code of files shared among projects, especially those at the lower code sharing level. Based on these findings, we suggest various maintenance strategies tailored to distinct levels of code sharing, along with potential avenues for future research.

To address this limitation, our approach divides the problem into two distinct phases - planning and implementation - to plan for a feasible trajectory and execute it once achieved, allowing for tighter control and better generalization. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on a latent code, it is possible to create new and unseen cell shape sequences. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated both qualitatively and quantitatively through comparisons of synthetic cells with actual cell growth, mitosis and lung cancer cells exhibiting complex protrusions. Our results demonstrate the generation of realistic synthetic cells with physiological topology structures, thereby providing a useful tool for creating training datasets for cell tracking and segmentation tasks.

Focusing on reinforcement learning methods that encourage agents to achieve target images without creating a 3D map, we examine this type of representation's capability to facilitate spatial tasks involving geometric consistency. The main contribution of this research is a detailed quantum equation outlining the concurrent behavior of a quantum system and a detector with limited capacity for information. Furthermore, by analyzing fast measurement rates, we derived a Markov-based equation focusing solely on the quantum system, capable of analytical analysis. The study is demonstrated by evaluating the fundamental mechanisms of two basic information conversion systems - one quantum and the other classical.

Our analysis reveals that changes in the wind pattern, characterized by a triangular area of reduced trade wind stress on the east side of the date line, are directly responsible for both types of El Ni\~no. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocities of binary star systems can be derived from publicly available electronic databases, which include the Hipparcos project's star data. By applying an appropriate correction for the refractive force of starlight, which can have a significant impact at low acceleration rates, the velocity distribution pattern of these binary star systems can be compared to predictions based on Newton's law of gravity. If the anomalous gravitational effect is scale-invariant and similar to the four-force phenomenon, which is not the case here, a clear discrepancy exists between the measured line velocities of these binary star systems and the predictions based on Newton's law of gravity. Instead, the measured line velocities are more in line with the general theory of relativity. To determine whether the star-refractive force correctly explains the measured line velocities, which in most cases is true, specific parameters of the star data, such as mass and distance, need to be accurately known. In general, the availability and precision of these parameters are sufficient to employ the star-refractive force as a viable gravitational effect model or to look for evidence of the four-force phenomenon.

To overcome these limitations, our approach utilizes ad visuals to enhance the performance of CTR prediction models. We achieve this by converting each ad into a set of visual identifiers that reflect its content. These identifiers are then used to generate visual embeddings, which can improve CTR predictions. The process of generating these visual identifiers is cast as a supervised quantization problem. Due to the absence of labels for commercial images, we instead utilize text descriptions to optimize our image extractor and create effective visual identifiers. Since traditional hard quantization operations are non-differentiable, we employ a softened quantization approach to support end-to-end network training. The resulting visual identifiers can then be paired with historical user-ad interactions to learn corresponding embeddings. Notably, the embedding derived from the visual content of an ad can effectively generalize to new ads. When used in conjunction with traditional ad behavior IDs, our approach leads to significantly improved performance, with average CTR increasing by 1.46% and total revenue rising by 1.10%.

semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using an equal-weighted loss function, disregarding the distinct importance of these labels. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. Moreover, we introduce a data augmentation step to refine the label set by reducing overfitting to the existing training data and increasing robustness against labeling errors. Experimental evaluations on six graph datasets demonstrate that InfoGNN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, yielding an average improvement of 6.17% and 4.63% in accuracy and F1-score, respectively.

Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of process magnitude, and the other describing the temporal occurrence of events given that magnitude. The second component is challenging due to the complex nature of event timings and thus far, methods like Gaussian and Dirichlet distributions have been used despite being oversimplified representations. Consequently, current methods fail to account for the actual underlying pattern of events in the process and thus lack clarity and versatility when dealing with intricate patterns. In order to tackle this issue, a new method based on the distribution of events via the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation is proposed, focusing on the inter-event intervals. The ILR depth measure is initially defined for a uniform Poisson process using a transformed space and its applicability is later extended to all point processes using time-rescaling techniques. The ILR depth's efficiency is showcased via simulations involving Poisson and non-Poisson processes, highlighting its superiority over existing approaches, while its theoretical properties and asymptotic analysis are also meticulously investigated. Ultimately, a practical case study confirms the effectiveness of this novel technique.

Utilizing a numerical code, we simulated a wide array of scenarios in which three protostars interacted, either as a solitary entity or in various binary and ternary configurations.  Our results indicate that in these systems, the lesser stars tend to acquire mass at a faster rate than the more massive ones, a phenomenon we refer to as mass inversion.  We observed mass inflation in systems consisting of a binary and a solitary star, a phenomenon we did not expect to occur as frequently as we anticipated, and found that in many cases, the outcomes of these interactions were complex and difficult to predict.

MA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary system's formation mass is influenced by its parent core's overall mass. In these simulations, they implemented azimuthally symmetric mass seeds within a rotating core, promoting the development of a dense filament, where a binary system might emerge. This binary formation process decreased as the core's mass increased, prompting researchers to amplify the core's kinetic energy ratio to its gravitational energy. This alteration led to increased binary mass and enabled a more precise determination of how a system's mass is generated. Furthermore, researchers created a diagram to represent binary system formation based on total core mass and kinetic energy ratio. This study also recorded and presented various properties of proto-stellar fragments, including formation mass, thermal to gravitational energy ratio, and kinetic energy ratio.

Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently heuristic. Within the context of a theoretical framework developed by Kraichnan, a new Hamiltonian-based analysis is applied to parquet's structure in the context of fermionic particles, resulting in a natural formation of the theory's underlying equations through its canonical representation. This approach reveals the inherent connection between the conserving properties of the derived scattering amplitude and the traditional parquet theory. Although the new analysis is initially applied to fermionic particles, its methodology can be extended to cover particles with multiple components and a range of interactions.

This phenomenon gives rise to a diverging density of states near the Fermi level at $T_c$ under zero pressure, but such divergence is avoided under a pressure greater than $p_c$ as the states near the Fermi level become occupied. Instead, a singular behavior emerges, characterized by a power-law dependence of the density of states, especially in three dimensions, given by $1 (\Delta \mu)^{1-d/2}$, where $\Delta \mu$ represents the binding energy of excitons. This description mirrors the singular behavior of the density of states that appears in superconductivity.

we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to calculate higher-order corrections for Kerr and Reissner-Nordström black holes, effectively recovering known results and presenting new insights.

requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to eliminate unnecessary information, leading to performance decline with increasing memory size.
To address this limitation, we introduce the Memory-Warping Network (MWN), which combines the capacity of dynamic memory and warping transformations to enable an agent to navigate to targeted areas and remember past navigation routes.
The MWN is comprised of a transformation module and a memory module that utilizes a set of flexible memory vectors.
The network's memory vectors can be distorted to store various forms of information, and the direction of warping can be controlled to optimize performance.
The output of the MWN's transformation module is projected onto a navigation map to determine the desired direction of warping, and the memory module's direction of warping is adjusted accordingly.
To train the MWN, we developed a new loss function that automatically learns to control the flexibility of memory vectors and maximizes the likelihood of optimal warping directions.
Experimental evaluations of our MWN on the MiniATARI and Atari games demonstrate its superior performance relative to four alternative methods.

fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The numerical framework of the fracture approach used in this study is thoroughly described.

AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and social studies. However, standard approaches to visual explanation are often insufficient due to their failure to account for the unique aspects of semantic segmentation tasks, which include skipping pixels, down-sampling, and ignoring spatial structure. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative synthetic evaluation technique that leverages generative models to create realistic datasets with varied properties, enabling a comprehensive assessment of segmentation models under control. By using controlled datasets, we are able to pinpoint and rectify a significant oversight in current methods related to completeness, i.e., their tendency to miss predicting certain pixels, particularly those located at the edges of objects. To achieve this goal, we employ a generative approach by combining a trained fully convolutional generative adversarial network with a sampling method, which allows us to create incomplete datasets with a wide range of completion patterns. Additionally, we introduce a novel metric called proportion of predicted pixels per class that helps us pinpoint areas where segmentation models are lacking in terms of local completeness. Experimenting with various synthetic datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving incomplete segmentation models through density-based neighborhood expansion, and showcase the benefits of our evaluation method by identifying and explaining a significant improvement in existing methods related to local completeness.

Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry, resulting in distinct electron and hole transports. These experiments reveal that interference enhances the thermoelectric power and efficiency of heat transfer from one direction to another. Furthermore, heat rectification can be achieved by adjusting an electric potential to create a specific energy level alignment. A theoretical model supports these findings and offers a framework for controlling heat in microscale devices through quantum physics.

SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. As a result, the world is relying heavily on public health precautions such as social distancing measures to curb the virus spread and maintain the healthcare system functionality. With the isolation of communities, access to reliable information has become restricted. Consequently, the health minister in South Africa updates the public every day on COVID-19 infections, including affected individuals' demographic and travel details. Meanwhile, the National Institute for Communicable Diseases provides daily updates on testing numbers, case counts, and fatality rates via infographics but often fails to release patients' ages or other critical transmission details. Recognizing the need to effectively share this information, the University of Pretoria's Data Science for Social Impact research team developed an open-access data platform comprising a data warehouse and an online dashboard, enabling transparent and efficient data sharing, including successful implementation of effective communication strategies. This experience highlighted the significance of data integration for public health and effective dissemination, prompting the team to address these challenges as they seek to apply their methods to other health-related issues in the future.

Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. Although higher-mass black holes have lower emission, the density of such black holes is also lower, meaning Hawking radiation temperature remains above the cosmic microwave background temperature. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations take unit time. The success of this foundation will be built upon demonstrating that a RAM with only basic addition operations can perform essential arithmetic operations efficiently after initial linear-time processing. Additionally, despite the limited storage capacity of individual registers ($O(N)$), it is feasible to handle larger integers by distributing them across a fixed number ($d$) of registers and leveraging surprising computational methods to execute a wide range of arithmetic operations on these 'polynomial' integers in constant time after initial linear preprocessing.

Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and this leads to a notable difference in their logarithmic power spectra in lower frequency regions. Although SGWMB's total power does not significantly contribute to the overall gravitational wave background due to its limited high-frequency cutoff, and this is primarily driven by the binary merger rate's limitations. As detector capabilities improve and the binary merger rate increases, so too will SGWMB's influence on the overall gravitational wave background.

This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, utilizing a lower supply voltage than recommended, to extend the time required for SRAM access and thereby generate higher-quality random numbers. To mitigate voltage-related reliability concerns, this design employs dual SRAM arrays and ensures that successful readings in both arrays are required to validate each generated random bit. As a result, this SRAM-based TRNG is capable of providing high-throughput entropy to applications, at the cost of a slightly reduced maximum operating frequency due to the requirement of dual SRAM readings. Furthermore, the implementation details of this design are discussed, specifically focusing on the necessary alterations to the SRAM timing specification. Experimental outcomes confirm the feasibility of this concept, demonstrating that increasing the access time results in totally distinct SRAM behavior and, therefore, higher-quality random numbers. Moreover, the implementation details of this design are discussed, showcasing its viability.

the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since networks cannot easily switch between tasks without compromising their performance. To address this issue, we developed an innovative method, 'Continual Kernel Adaptation Network (CKAN)', enabling simultaneous training of networks and their kernels to facilitate seamless task transitions and maintain expertise across various tasks. CKAN's effectiveness was validated through kernel analysis, classification experiments, and comparisons with other established methods. Notably, our approach outperformed the competition by retaining up to 95% of each network's expertise on initial tasks while maintaining 100% of its knowledge on subsequent tasks, demonstrating superior multi-task accuracy. To facilitate easy integration with existing training pipelines, we also released an open-source Python toolkit, 'CKAN-Net', along with detailed documentation and a set of tutorials. This toolkit allows researchers to replicate our findings and experiment with other state-of-the-art methods.

For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. We investigate four primary questions by developing a custom dataset for sharing knowledge among models and analyzing their performance under different pretraining conditions. Our findings indicate that a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects a model's ability to learn in-context, with variations in domain leading to a 10-fold difference in performance. Interestingly, we discovered that a pretraining corpus's size mainly impacts the model's ability to generalize outside its domain of origin, with larger pretraining corpora resulting in lower ability to generalize outside the domain of origin. These findings suggest that a pretraining corpus's size and domain are unrelated to each other, with the size affecting the model's ability to generalize outside the domain of origin. We further discovered shared factors responsible for the model's ability to learn in-context across various scenarios and found that a pretraining corpus's domain is primarily associated with the model's ability to learn in-context in domains similar to its own, with a pretraining corpus's size being associated with the model's ability to learn in-context outside its domain of origin.

To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the surrounding hot intracluster medium before ultimately fragmenting and creating numerous smaller clumps. These fragments act as nuclei, fostering further condensation through processes including Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, thereby nearly doubling the cold gas mass within a 75 million-year period. Cloud expansion appears to be determined by factors such as density and local heat removal, with greater fragmentation allowing more extensive growth. Magnetic fields are found to have a moderating effect on the growth of these clouds, restricting growth in highly fragmented areas while promoting it in fields with lower strength. Magnetic fields also seem to impede the merging of cold clumps, with fewer strong magnetic fields allowing for more mergers to occur, thus influencing the mass distribution of these clumps. Magnetic fields may have a similar effect on the formation of these clumps on a smaller scale, with numerical models indicating similar processes could occur on a cooler, kiloparsec scale. Our findings on these clumps could provide valuable insights for future telescope observations, such as James Webb Space Telescope, which will be capable of detecting these cold components on a smaller scale

Initially, we've formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach has far-reaching implications, as any resource-limited transformation becomes achievable via a series of discrete steps, each involving the conversion of a general quantum state into a state within a specific resource-limited subset.
By adapting a graph-theoretic framework, we've demonstrated that the task of geometric transformation, or mapping one quantum state into another within a certain distance from a reference state, can be accurately represented.
This approach has enabled us to derive both a general upper bound and a more restrictive lower bound for the minimum number of conversions required for achieving a resource-constrained transformation.
These results have significant implications, as applying them to previously proposed protocols for state manipulation has led to the discovery of more accurate approximations and novel lower bounds for essential resource costs.

This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle.

aviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G-actions' Schreier graphs. We then explore the Schreier growth gap for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a finitely generated torsion-free norm, but is not virtually abelian, it exhibits a Schreier growth gap of n^3. We also establish that solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank have a Schreier growth gap of n^α for some real number α less than two. To establish these results, we introduce a generalization of nilpotent groups, called centralised nilpotent groups, and prove that every finite-valued centralised nilpotent group has a Schreier growth gap of n^2.

The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns.

(ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing large sets of artificially generated data, it's shown that ML algorithms can successfully predict measurement uncertainties without seeing the data itself. However, the parameterizations of uncertainty that work best on artificially generated data may not work as well in real-world scenarios, highlighting the need for more sophisticated models of uncertainty. By employing numerical validation techniques, it's confirmed that accurately formulating the law of gravity and accounting for drag forces using ML methods is possible. However, significant breakthroughs in theoretical discrepancy models and secondary physical mechanisms are needed to take physics-informed machine learning beyond simulation and into the realm of experimental validation.

their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, also known as Bonsai, which comprises a sequence of iterative training episodes. Predicting the bulk modulus of this matter is complicated due to its fragile connection with other properties of dense matter. However, by using the general relation between the bulk modulus and pressure, we can investigate the required precision in pressure and bulk modulus estimates needed to replicate star gravitational radius measurements made through lensing and shape measurements. For a 1.4 solar mass star, we find the bulk modulus can be estimated with a precision of around 25-30% to replicate star gravitational radius measurements made through shape measurements, and as little as 10-20% to replicate lensing measurements. This precision need not be met in its entirety, as it can be compensated for by differences in star mass and radius. Eventually, our findings may aid in constraining the equation of state from gravitational wave observations of binary neutron star mergers and their impact on post-merger emission.

Early-type U galaxies shared certain characteristics with late-type S galaxies, whereas late-type U galaxies were more similar to type-changing U galaxies. We're interested in the fundamental properties of harmonic functions in these manifolds, such that their functions are distinct from constants. Our key contribution lies in the demonstration of two key bounds for these functions: first, we've established a maximum boundary value for these functions; second, we've derived a mean value inequality for these functions. Our method of calculation is straightforward and easily applicable. We've also established that, in certain situations, harmonic functions can achieve the maximum possible value at the boundary of the manifold. We've also provided an alternative way of looking at the mean value inequality, such that it relates to the Laplacian of these functions at specific points within the manifold. We've further generalized our results to apply not just to harmonic functions, but also to more advanced functions, such as $k$-harmonic functions. We've demonstrated that our new inequalities can provide insights into the fundamental properties of these $k$-harmonic functions, such as their behavior at the boundary of the manifold, including when they $k$-constant. We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain and actions taken by the imitation policy.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and actions to facilitate this correspondence.  Additionally, the framework incorporates a geometry-aware loss to ensure symmetry in the learned transformation, thereby enabling the imitation policy to utilize the expert domain's geometry to perform imitation.  The proposed method is verified to be effective through experiments across a diverse range of multi-task imitation tasks.

An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not. the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are actually not gravitationally bound. Furthermore, we found that these structures' ages, when compared to their actual age spread, appear excessively large. It is also worth noting that these structures, while seemingly homogeneous, can exhibit identical characteristics if composed of randomly selected stars from separate clusters, indicating that these structures' properties do not necessarily indicate a physically connected state. Ultimately, based on these findings, we cannot rule out the possibility that these structures represent a genuine phenomenon requiring new theoretical explanations or if they simply represent an effective method for identifying and studying stellar populations.

quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse methods to quantify specific quantum effects. It plays a pivotal role in the theoretical foundation of quantum physics and engineering. The concept of reversibility has been a central idea in this theory, allowing researchers to identify resources within purely theoretical systems. Nevertheless, this idea is difficult to apply in experiments, often resulting in the destruction of valuable resources. This study proposes an alternative approach to determine free states and operations that can be utilized to implement quantum resource theories experimentally. The methodology is based on minimizing resource creation and preserving operations' efficiency. The largest possible operational distance to free states and the maximal efficiency of bi-partite incoherent channels are established as the criteria for measuring resource creation and preservation, respectively. We demonstrate the practical potential of this approach by evaluating the remaining resource after single-shot data acquisition and implementing it to obtain the minimal amount of resource creation in channels. Moreover, our method is experimentally verified using superconducting qubits and reveals valuable information about the remaining resource even with moderate multi-use scenarios. This approach offers a practical means of managing quantum resources during actual experiments.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. A potential drawback is that a false negative declaration by the filter may allow an unauthorized access attempt. To supplement Bloom filters, many systems use additional safety measures, but these often require adjustable safety levels, speeds, and memory allocations, all of which must be set ahead of time. Our solution involves replacing traditional Bloom filters with directed bipartite graphs to manage membership testing, allowing us to include false positives and take advantage of graphic data structures' efficient preimage recovery capabilities. Specifically, we propose using regular graphs and minimizing vertex degrees to optimize performance and memory usage. Our implementation includes a revised Bloom filter that can operate without a prior estimate of the desired false positive rate, forcing such estimates in standard Bloom filters can risk inadequate performance. Our tests demonstrate that our new Bloom filters offer notable performance gains over traditional Bloom filters, particularly when recovering preimages are involved. Notably, our solution can adapt to dynamic data without compromising performance, a capability it achieves by dynamically adjusting the bipartite graph's structure to optimize memory usage and recovery speed.

2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-time applications.
To address this issue, the OOV challenge combined the forces of three leading datasets from the OCR community: ImageNet, ICDAR2013, and LIQUIDDB.
The challenge consisted of a two-stage selection process: first, the task required participants to identify whether a given image contained the same text as a reference image, and second, if confirmed, to extract the corresponding text.
The event featured two distinct categories: the Incidental Category, which represented text occurrences that were fewer than 10 occurrences in the reference dataset, and the Common Occurrence Category, which was defined by the presence of text occurring more than 10 times in the reference dataset.
In the final evaluation stage, our team OOVCROS, comprised of three members, secured first and second places in both categories, demonstrating a 0.916 AUC score in the Incidental Category and a 0.934 AUC score in the Common Occurrence Category.

Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and significant memory requirements. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively reducing memory needs during training. Our proposed framework, MemNet, incorporates a novel architecture of grouped CNN layers and an optimized memory allocation scheme, enabling training with a significantly lower memory footprint without compromise performance. Through extensive experiments on standard image classification datasets, MemNet has demonstrated up to 24 times reduction in memory consumption while achieving only minor, 3.07%, reduction in top-1 accuracy, and retaining similar computational efficiency.

avitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. Due to its reduced complexity and ability to operate at high speeds, this method is well-suited for real-time application in future gravitational wave detectors.

Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this model, the proposed iterative algorithm has been mathematically justified and verified with numerical reconstructions of a cylinder and a human pelvis acquired using an X-ray source with multiple energy levels.

A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for the creation of scalable, high-performance applications that can adapt to changing GPU hardware configurations.  To demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, we successfully applied it to a variety of real-world SMMO applications, including graph algorithms, logic inferences, and numerical analyses, achieving notable performance gains up to 2.4 times faster than leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C absolute error, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C.

In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. This study presents a new technique for creating entangled photons with controllable polarization, utilizing a quantum dot and microcavity system. By designing a microcavity with an octagonal shape and incorporating a dot at its center, researchers achieved spontaneous four-wave mixing, producing entangled photons without the need for postselection or massive photon emission. Characterization of the generated entanglement led to the observation of Bell exponentials and demonstrated its potential in studying quantum optics phenomena and applications.

Initially, the upper bound for online Euclidean spanners in 0-dimensional space (sequences) was established by Alon and others in 1982, and it seemed to be closely related to the combinatorial complexity of the sequence. However, Dubash and Chechik introduced a counterexample in 2018 showing that the previous bound could be achieved using a simple, combinatorial algorithm. This paper addresses a generalization of this problem to multi-dimensional spaces by providing a tight (up to a logarithmic factor) upper bound for the cost of online Euclidean spanners in 0-dimensional space, and extending it to 1-dimensional space and plane space. The new upper bound is close to being tight, and it compares the cost of online Euclidean spanners to the minimum number of edges required to form a geometric network in these spaces.

This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. Research has shown that magnetic bright points contribute a significant amount of energy to the solar corona, with the question of their role in coronal heating still requiring further investigation. The task involves analyzing data from the Solar Optical Telescope on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, captured in high-cadence mode over two days, to obtain precise measurements of the bright points' sizes, distances, and velocities. The resulting data contain hundreds of magnetic bright points, with measurements showing their velocities typically range from 0.5 to 0.8 km/s, while some feature velocities exceeding 1 km/s. Consequently, the dark monopole's density in the universe is predicted to be lower than the existing proton density by at least two orders of magnitude, thereby potentially resolving the matter-antimatter asymmetry. The required mass of the dark particle is estimated to be greater than the proton mass. The existence of these dark magnetic monopoles would give rise to three distinct types of astronomical phenomena: transient stellar ablations, permanent stellar acceleration, and gamma-ray bursts. These phenomena could serve as early indicators of the presence of dark magnetic monopoles.

we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. Our recent joint research with Charles Fefferman established a principle that enables the existence of a Lipschitz selection for $F$, which is a mapping $f:{\mathcal M}\to X$ that satisfies $f(x)\in F(x)$ for every $x\in{\mathcal M}$. a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple.

our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. In this case, we identify tight lower and upper bounds for the more general leakage metric through the application of single-letter analysis.

This approach involves initially generating an ensemble of states on a quantum circuit, followed by selecting a few instances based on their quantum status, and finally a classical process of perturbing the best quantum instances to produce candidate solutions.  To improve the efficiency of this algorithm, we first examine the quantum status measure, then suggest a strategy to reduce the number of expensive classical operations required.  This method entails utilizing an easier-to-compute metric to select the best quantum instances, and testing the resulting solutions through a classical phase.  The improved QAOA is compared to the standard version by evaluating its performance on the Maximum Cut problem applied to a specific type of random graph.  The results indicate that the enhanced scheme yields higher probability outcomes, and initial findings suggest that this algorithmic variation can be expanded to solve more intricate optimization problems.

The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. This study applies the mathematical and topological structure of Markovian models to demonstrate the gauge invariance of the normalized cumulant-generating function. By taking advantage of this invariance, we have developed a streamlined method for the practical calculation of asymptotic averages and kth-order cumulants of observables. This method is versatile and can be adapted to deal with both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the asymptotic regime of the cumulant-generating function corresponds to the equilibrium state, characterized by an equilibrium potential. By introducing the concept of 'path cumulants', we have also shown that the stochastic thermodynamic model's behavior in the kth-order cumulant regime can be equivalent to that of the harmonic mean. Notably, our work includes specific case studies, including finite-state models and Gaussian Markov processes. These examples not only illustrate the application of our method but also reveal similarities between the cumulative distribution function and the probability density function.

Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope, with wavelengths of 0.48 and 2.1 microns, are presented during a period of reduced dust activity, revealing a refined upper limit of the planet's radius of approximately 4500 km. Medium-depth transit observations also suggest particle sizes ranging from 0.5 to 1 micron, suggesting extremely high mass loss rates of about 3e8 kg/s, coherent with hydrodynamic escape theories. In contrast, explosive volcanic eruptions or other mechanisms generating this activity would demand exceptional geological activity levels. Combining these results with the maximum possible planetary size, our findings estimate the remaining lifespan of the exoplanet at approximately 370 million years; conversely, incorporating predictions from hydrodynamical models yields a remarkably reduced lifespan of only 21 million years.

influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same.

The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access powerful computing tools more efficiently.
